Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and other Members of the Committee,
My name is Butch Russell and I'm speaking today on behalf of the Maine Ambulance Association. We represent EMS agencies across the state, including those that serve Maine's island communities.
We're here in strong support of LD 841. This bill takes an important step toward addressing the serious challenges island communities face when trying to get emergency care to their residents.
We've heard from many island communities in recent years that it's becoming harder to safely and quickly transport patients to the mainland. Vinalhaven, for example, is fortunate to have regular ferry service--but when the ferry isn't running, they, like many smaller islands including Cranberry Isles, rely on local fishermen to get the job done. This kind of improvising speaks to the strength and resourcefulness of these communities, but it also shows how fragile and inconsistent the current system can be.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished colleagues of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, my name is Chip Curry. I represent Senate District 11, which encompasses all 26 rural, coastal, and island communities ofWaldo County. Thank you for the opportunity to present LD 841, "Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service Effects on Island Communities in the State."
This is a timely and targeted proposal that stems from two ongoing conversations -- one in the Legislature and one unfolding in real time in our coastal communities.
In recent years, the Legislature has devoted considerable energy and attention to the challenges facing our state's emergency medical services. We've studied the EMS workforce crisis, the collapse of rural and volunteer-based EMS systems, and the rising demands placed on a patchwork of under-resourced responders. This committee has taken those concerns seriously -- and I know many of you have sat through hours of testimony from fire chiefs, EMTs, and town officials, all of whom have described a system under strain.
LD 841 builds on that foundation by directing a working group to focus on a specific but critical aspect of that crisis: EMS access in Maine's island communities.
As the Committee may be aware, the Department of Transportation and the Maine State Ferry Service have recently floated the idea of changing overnight ferry berthing from the islands to the mainland. While the intent is to improve operational efficiency and address workforce needs, islanders, including my constituents, have sounded the alarm about what this shift could mean for emergency medical care.
As the Bangor Daily News and multiple outlets reported just a few months ago, local officials from Islesboro, North Haven, and other communities fear that losing an overnight ferry presence could delay response times in life-threatening situations.' For years, the ferry system has quietly played a backup role in emergency response -- transporting patients and EMTs in off hours when every minute matters. If the ferries are no longer stationed on the island, who fills that gap? LifeFlight? Local volunteers? New emergency vessels? What are the costs, and what solutions are sustainable?

This isn't a duplication of prior studies; rather, it's a focused extension. Donald Pearson North Haven; Southern Harbor Elder Services LD 841
I strongly oppose the proposed change to originate and end North Haven ferry runs on the mainland. It will add at least an hour -- likely more depending on crew availability and readiness, vessel startup process and weather -- to emergency evacuations from the island. Lacking ferry transport, either an airplane or a smaller island-berthed vessel would be required.
The landing facilities for the former require an access agreement with a private landowner or, lacking that, use of a meandering grass landing strip after negotiating a tricky approach over power lines.
Evacuation by a smaller vessel, assuming crew availability and decent weather, requires suitable docking at the prevailing tide and exacting manual patient transport to the vessel under potentially dangerous conditions underfoot in prevailing weather. Needless to say, the patient is subject to significant exposure and to the possibility of additional injury during transport.

Testimony in support of LD 841: Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service E ects on Island Communities in the State by Jonnathan Busko MD. April 2, 2025
Dear Senator Bebee-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and esteemed members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee,
My name is Jonnathan Busko and I live in Bangor. I am testifying today to urge you to support LD 841. With almost 20 years of working with island communities regarding health services access, I see this resolve as finally bringing the issue of access to emergency services to a level at which a comprehensive and sustainable solution can be identified.
I am an EMS and emergency physician. Over the last 2 decades, I've worked intermittently with several island communities regarding access to healthcare services. I was the Maine EMS Region 4 medical director for 11 years. In that role, I participated in workgroups of island EMS services, all of whom identify sta ing and transportation barriers to care. From 2019-2022, I was the medical director for Boothbay Region Ambulance Service, a shore-based EMS service that worked in conjunction with the US Coast Guard to provide EMS services to Monhegan Island until January 2024. I've been the medical advisor for Monhegan First Aid since its inception in 2020, supporting the community to provide first aid services throughout the summer season. Over the past 18 years I've participated in workgroups to discuss shared transport services amongst the islands, such as an ambulance boat.
These days much of my job is to work with rural and frontier communities in Maine to help them identify their top priority health services access needs and then develop solutions to those needs. In the last 2 years I've conducted assessments on Monhegan Island, Vinalhaven Island, Isle au Haut, and Swan's Island. Access to emergency care / EMS, whether by establishing new EMS services or stabilizing or enhancing existing services is consistently in the top 5 priorities in these communities.
I believe that the study proposed by LD 841 o ers a meaningful opportunity to identify the challenges faced by island communities to access EMS services as well as to develop a shared, e icient, and sustainable model for delivering these services. However, both through my experience from the community surveys as well as my current participation on a Maine Seacoast Mission advisory committee on telehealth services, I've seen that island communities are struggling with health services access in general. I led a Maine EMS approved Pilot Project called the Critical Access Physician Extender program in Jackman in which enhanced EMS services were provided in the community. During the 29-month pilot period, the Critical Access Integrated Paramedics provided 383 paramedic EMS responses in partnership with Jackman Moose River Fire Rescue. However, they also provided non-emergency care services, performing 96 community paramedicine visits and 145 facilitated tele-urgent care visits, saving patients almost 20,000 miles of travel. While I'm not advocating for this specific model, I am saying that EMS agencies are the touchstone of healthcare in every community, they are able to provide vital non-emergency services in their communities, and many island communities are hurting for access to any health services. Given this, I would encourage you to consider the following modifications to the charge to the committee and to the committee membership.

Testimony in support of LD 841: Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service E ects on Island Communities in the State by Jonnathan Busko MD. April 2, 2025
1. Modify the charge for the workgroup as follows: "...shall convene a working group to study the delivery of emergency medical services to and ferry service e ects on island communities in the State, to include consideration of the sustainability of EMS services and their potential role in delivering non-emergency healthcare services to island communities."
2. Add a member identified as "A representative of an island community that is currently not served by a community-based EMS service." There are several islands that do not currently have licensed EMS services and care is often provided on an ad hoc basis by community members who have some level of first aid or medical training. The needs of these island communities are di erent than those of island communities with EMS services.
3. Add a member identified as "A representative of an island community that has a community-based health care facility sta ed by licensed independent practitioners (e.g. physicians, physician assistants, or nurse practitioners)." The needs of these communities are also potentially significantly di erent from those of a community with only an EMS service or no medical services. For example, on Vinalhaven Island, Islands Community Medical Services has historically been identified by Maine EMS as one of two non-hospital receiving facilities in Maine for EMS transports; that is, Vinalhaven EMS may transport appropriate patients to the on-island clinic rather than having to transport them to mainland hospitals. Additionally, on some islands where there are clinics, the provider sta respond on EMS calls, resulting in provider level care which decreases the need for transport for some patients.
Finally, I would suggest deciding if you intend to have this work group focus on all island communities, or only the unbridged island communities. While I recognize that with more extreme weather events even bridged island communities are finding themselves intermittently isolated from the mainland, this problem is primarily one for unbridged, year-round communities and I would suggest that language (unbridged year-round) should be added to the resolve where appropriate.
I appreciate your consideration of this important issue.
Jonnathan Busko MD MPH MBA

I am writing to testify that without access to a ferry docked on-island over night, the safety and sustainability of our year-round community will be drastically impacted.
North Haven island is growing. Unlike the population of our state as a whole, the population of North Haven island is growing larger and growing younger. This is positive and promising for the sustainability of our island and island populations in general.
The ferry boat not being accessible at night for emergency services could change this all. Most families on North Haven do not own their own lobster boats. That helps our K-12 school, our community center, our island market and restaurants, our library, and our EMS and Fire crews remaiun sustainable. That could change immediately with this decision. This decision will, without a doubt affect every aspect of our island trajectory.
It is important to understand that unbridged islands are fragile ecosystems and this decision could collapse ours completely.

10041530:
LD841 Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service Effects on Island Communities in the State
Testimony in Support
April 2, 2025
Senator Beebe- Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the Criminal Justice & Public Safety Committee, my name is Kimberly Grindle and I am a resident of Islesboro. I am submitting this letter today to express my support for LD 841, "Resolve, To Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service Effects on Island Communities in the State."
I am a 7th generation island resident. My children, other immediate family members, and I have all used the ferry during medical emergencies. However, we have also been forced to rely on a lobster boat, our island's water taxi, and even LifeFlight of Maine when the ferry was unable-- or unwilling--to transport us. Unfortunately, the trend seems to be that the ferry system does not want to support island residents, visitors, or workers during "off-hour" medical emergencies by choosing not to transport a person while in the midst of a medical emergency. While they do sometimes make trips, there is no consistency, and the reality is that having the boat berthed on the mainland overnight could have disastrous effects.
Essential, reliable ferry transportation and timely emergency services are vital to the health and safety of our communities. These systems are lifelines--not just for routine travel, but for critical care, including trauma response, chronic illness management, and childbirth. Most rural EMT crews are volunteer-based and asking these volunteers to risk dangerous waters in small vessels--especially during increasingly stormy winters--is not safe. It is less ideal for the patient being transported. LifeFlight is an option, but too often, their aircraft is unavailable due to other calls, or weather conditions prevent them from flying. Even when transport is possible, patients that are not covered by health insurance are then faced with a nearly $20,000 bill.
This bill is a necessary step toward forward in gaining valuable insight into the strengths and weaknesses of our current system. More importantly, this study can help guide future policy decisions to ensure that island residents have timely, reliable access to the medical services they need. I strongly urge you to support LD 841.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

To: Senator Pinny Beebe-Center and Representative Tavis Hasenfus Chairs, and Members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee
Re: Testimony about LD 841 to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services and Ferry Service Effects on 27 island communities in the State
My name is Martin Phillips. I am a retired physician, and have been spending about 5 months of the summer on Islesboro, a large island in Penobscot Bay for about 15 years. We have a terrific community there, and we have deep friendships with both seasonal and year-round residents from all walks of life.
At the end of 2021 the Emergency Medical Service on the island needed more Emergency Medical Technicians. I thought that after having a career in medicine which included some work in emergency rooms, getting an EMT license would be easy, and I could basically walk on to the ambulance.
Well, I discovered that it wasn't that easy. I studied hard, taking a lot of time, to learn the many techniques and skills that an EMT needs that are very different from the practice of medicine in a hospital.
I have taken as many shifts as my schedule allows, mostly weekends and a few nights. It is incredibly rewarding, because as an EMT you are dropped into someone else's life at one of their lowest moments, and you do everything in your power to help them and get them to definitive care. I have helped a mother whose baby stopped breathing, people having heart attacks and strokes, people in pain, with broken bones, and an older man with dementia who could no longer be safe alone in his house.
These events don't happen 9 to 5 or on anyone's schedule. That is the topic of our request today. When we are transporting a critical patient, the ferry has been a godsend. We drive the ambulance on to the ferry, and continue caring for the patient without interruption, just like we are on the highway. The crews and captains are heroes.
We have a protocol so that we only call for the ferry when it is needed. If a patient is stable enough, we take them by private boat and meet an ambulance at the Lincolnville Ferry dock. If they are critical, we call Life Flight, if they can fly. But for unstable patients, seamless access to the ferry at night is lifesaving.
I have great respect for our Service Chief, Fred Porter who runs a very professional organization, for my colleagues on the truck, and the Health Center team who pitch in. Maintaining a first-class EMS to serve the people on a remote island needs the close coordination of many moving pieces.
I strongly request that we continue to dock the ferry on Islesboro overnight, and urge this Committee to vote "Ought to pass." Thank you.

Good morning Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety. I am Representative Michael Ray, and I represent the towns of Appleton, Islesboro, Liberty, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont in House District 40. I'm writing in strong support of LD 841 : Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry Service Effects on Island Communities in the State.
Emergency medical services are at risk throughout the state, and current and prior Legislatures have made and are making positive steps in addressing this situation. I believe that the people of the State of Maine will be better served - and lives saved- because of this attention. However, while the reliance on an ambulance is vital no matter where one lives, residents on islands currently face an even more uncertain future. With most often a stretch of open water between themselves and a hospital, island communities present a unique challenge. And so I encourage the creation of a working group focused on island needs and conditions to study how we might meet that challenge.
While just about anyone calling a Maine island home would proudly say that their piece of ground is unique, islands across the country and globe have looked at how ferries affect EMS services. I'm sure there are many, many areas ripe for inquiry. I believe a focused study will bring to light many alternatives to currently a most worrisome situation.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Testimony in Support of LD 841 Resolve, to Study the Delivery of Emergency Medical Services to and Ferry
Service Effects on Island Communities in the State
Good morning, Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee. My name is Rick Petrie, and I am a Paramedic and the Chief Executive Officer for North East MoBHeTTealth, an Ambulance Service based in Saco Maine. Previously, I served as the Regional EMS Director for the area covering the Coast and Islands for 21 years.
I was fortunate to serve as a member of the EMS Blue Ribbon Committee and have been working with the Island EMS agencies for many years on the escalating patient transport problem.
Every time the tones go off for an Emergency Medical Call on the Islands, one of the responders has the job of planning the logistics of patient transport. Currently, the primary system available to many of the islands, the Ferry Service, is strained by workforce and operational issues. LifeFlight of Maine is a key component of the transport algorithm but should be resen/ed for the most critically ill or injured patients. Other players in the system; Penobscot Air, Coast Guard, Marine Patrol are constrained with their own operational issues. Many times, the responders must rely on the goodwill of local lobster and personal boat owners to step up to help their neighbors.
It is important for the Legislature to convene this working group to look at a system that would reduce the burden on the Ferry service and develop a more consistent, reliable and patient-centric system for the transport of emergency medical patients from the islands to the hospitals on the mainland. There are models available that could not only reach this goal but can also provide Emergency Medical Support services to Island Communities that are currently under-resourced.
Thank you for your consideration, and I am happy to answer any questions you may
have.

I am a retired RN and have an understanding of community safety and health needs. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely Wendy Springborn.
